etymology: A Hebraism rendered literally into Greek at Luke 10:6 — huios eirēnēs ("son of peace"). The Semitic idiom "son of X" denotes a person characterized by X; a "son of peace" is one disposed to receive the messengers of the gospel of peace.
biblical_def: The "son of peace" is the receptive person the Lord Jesus instructs the seventy to look for as they enter each town in Luke 10:1-12. The instruction is precise: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house. And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again" (Luke 10:5-6). The phrase is a Hebraism — "son of X" meaning "one characterized by X" — rendered woodenly into Greek, so that "son of peace" means a person already disposed by grace to receive the messengers of the gospel of peace (Eph 6:15). The concept functions as a readiness filter, not a rejection of the lost: the messengers preach to the whole town, but they invest their lodging, their depth, and their continuing labor in the household that receives them. Where the message is refused, they shake off the dust and move on (Luke 10:10-11). From the Reformed standpoint, the son of peace is one in whom the Spirit has already begun the work of effectual calling, so that the outward proclamation meets an inwardly-prepared heart (Acts 16:14, "whose heart the Lord opened"). The doctrine does not license the church to preach only to the receptive; it licenses the church to allocate its depth toward the receptive while keeping the proclamation universal.
webster_summary: The receptive person the seventy are told to find in each town (Luke 10:6); a Hebraism for one disposed by grace to receive the gospel of peace; a readiness filter for allocating discipleship depth, not a restriction on proclamation.
webster_full: SON OF PEACE, noun phrase. Hebraism rendered into Greek at Luke 10:6 (huios eirēnēs).
The receptive householder the seventy are instructed to find as they enter each town (Luke 10:1-12).

Reformed reading: the son of peace is one in whom the Spirit has begun effectual calling, so outward proclamation meets an inwardly-prepared heart (Acts 16:14).

Acts 16:14
And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Ephesians 6:15

John 6:44

corruption_summary: The son of peace is corrupted when read as a pragmatic church-growth target-market filter that justifies preaching only to the receptive, when divorced from the Spirit's prior work of effectual calling, or when the readiness it names is attributed to the natural goodness of the receptive person rather than to grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Market-segmentation misreading. Modern church-growth strategy sometimes lifts the son of peace as a demographic-targeting principle: find your receptive audience and ignore the rest. The text refuses this. The seventy preach the kingdom to the whole town (Luke 10:8-9); the son of peace governs where they lodge and invest depth, not whether the gospel is proclaimed. Even the town that refuses is warned that the kingdom has come near (Luke 10:11). Allocation of depth is not restriction of proclamation.

Natural-receptivity misreading. The son of peace is sometimes read as a person whose own openness, sincerity, or spiritual seeking makes him receptive — as though the readiness were the man's native virtue. The Reformed reading anchors the readiness in grace: the Lord opened Lydia's heart (Acts 16:14); no man comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The son of peace is receptive because the Spirit has gone ahead of the messenger. The doctrine magnifies prevenient grace, not natural goodness.
roots_summary: Hebraism ("son of X" = "one characterized by X") rendered into Greek at Luke 10:6; the receptive householder the seventy are told to find; a readiness filter grounded in the Spirit's prior work of effectual calling.

etymology: From Luke 10:1, where the Lord Jesus appoints hebdomēkonta ("seventy"; some manuscripts "seventy-two") and sends them ahead of Him two by two. Distinct from the Twelve (Luke 9), and from the seventy elders of Numbers 11 and the Sanhedrin's seventy.
biblical_def: The Seventy are the wider band of disciples whom the Lord Jesus appointed and sent out two by two, ahead of His own face, into every city and place where He Himself would come (Luke 10:1). Their commission in Luke 10:1-12 parallels and extends the earlier sending of the Twelve (Luke 9:1-6): they are to travel light, to pronounce peace on each house, to find the son of peace, to heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God has come near, and to shake off the dust against any town that refuses them. The number seventy (or seventy-two in some manuscripts) likely echoes the seventy elders Moses appointed to share the burden of leadership (Num 11:16-17, 24-25) and the seventy nations of Genesis 10 — signaling that the mission reaches beyond Israel toward all the families of the earth. Their return is marked by joy: "Lord, even the devils are subject unto us through thy name" (Luke 10:17), to which the Lord responds with the warning to rejoice rather that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). The Seventy demonstrate the pattern this article's parent themes describe: broad proclamation (every city) paired with selective depth (lodging with the son of peace). They are the New Testament's model of a sent, multiplying, kingdom-announcing band that is larger than the inner Twelve yet still trained, commissioned, and accountable.
webster_summary: The wider band of disciples (Luke 10:1) the Lord Jesus sent two by two ahead of Him to announce the kingdom; distinct from the Twelve; their number echoes the seventy elders of Numbers 11 and the seventy nations of Genesis 10.
webster_full: THE SEVENTY, noun phrase. From Luke 10:1 (hebdomēkonta; some manuscripts seventy-two).
The wider band of disciples appointed and sent two by two, ahead of the Lord, into every city He would visit.
Commission (Luke 10:1-12): travel light, pronounce peace, find the son of peace, heal the sick, announce the kingdom, shake off dust against refusers.
Number echoes the seventy elders of Numbers 11 and the seventy nations of Genesis 10; distinct from the Twelve and from the Sanhedrin's seventy.
scriptures: Luke 10:1
After these things the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come.
Luke 10:2
Therefore said he unto them, The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few: pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he would send forth labourers into his harvest.
Luke 10:17

Luke 10:20
Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
corruption_summary: The Seventy are corrupted when their sending is read as proof that all believers hold the apostolic office, when their miraculous authority is treated as the normal continuing endowment of every disciple, or when their joy over power is elevated above the Lord's correction to rejoice in salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: Office-flattening misreading. Charismatic and restorationist movements sometimes cite the Seventy to argue that the sending and miraculous authority given to them is the standing endowment of every believer in every age. The text presents the Seventy as a specific historical sending tied to the Lord's own itinerant ministry and to the foundational announcement of the kingdom's arrival. The Reformed-cessationist reading distinguishes the foundational, sign-accompanied mission of the apostolic age from the ordinary means-of-grace ministry of the church now. The harvest-prayer (Luke 10:2) and the model of sent, accountable labor remain; the sign-gifts served the foundation.

Power-over-salvation misreading. The Seventy returned rejoicing that the devils were subject to them (Luke 10:17). The Lord redirected their joy: "rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20). Movements that center spiritual power, deliverance ministry, and dramatic authority over demons invert the Lord's own ordering. The ground of Christian joy is election unto salvation (names written in heaven), not the exercise of spiritual power. To rejoice chiefly in power is the very thing the Lord corrected.

etymology: From the Lord Jesus's words at Matthew 7:6, "neither cast ye your pearls before swine." The Greek margaritēs ("pearl") and choiros ("swine") form a proverb about the right allocation of sacred things. The idiom has passed into common English for wasting something valuable on those unable to esteem it.
biblical_def: "Pearls before swine" is the Lord Jesus's proverb at Matthew 7:6: "Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you." The saying teaches that holy things — the gospel, the deep things of God, sacred correction, the discipleship of the Word — are to be allocated with discernment, not scattered indiscriminately upon those who have shown themselves contemptuous and hostile. It is the counterweight, within the same Sermon on the Mount, to the command not to judge hypocritically (Matt 7:1-5): the disciple is neither to be censorious nor to be naive. The "dogs" and "swine" are not the merely lost (to whom the gospel is freely preached) but those who, having heard, respond with trampling contempt and turning violence. The verse pairs with the Lord's instruction to the Seventy to shake the dust off against a town that refuses them (Luke 10:10-11) and with Paul and Barnabas turning from persistent rejecters toward receptive soil (Acts 13:46). From the Reformed standpoint, the proverb governs the stewardship of sacred things: the gospel is proclaimed to all, but the depth of discipleship, the holy correction, and the sustained investment are allocated toward those who will not trample them. It is a wisdom-text about allocation, not a license for elitism or for withholding the gospel from sinners.
webster_summary: The Lord Jesus's proverb (Matt 7:6) that holy things are to be allocated with discernment, not scattered upon the contemptuous and hostile; a wisdom-text about stewarding sacred things, paired with the dust-shaking of Luke 10 and Paul's turn to receptive soil in Acts 13.

Proverb teaching the discerning allocation of holy things — not scattered upon those who trample them with contempt.
Counterweight, within the Sermon on the Mount, to the command against hypocritical judging (Matt 7:1-5): neither censorious nor naive.
The "dogs" and "swine" are those who, having heard, respond with trampling contempt and turning violence — not the merely lost, to whom the gospel is freely preached.

corruption_summary: Pearls before swine is corrupted when twisted into a license to withhold the gospel from sinners, when used to justify spiritual elitism or contempt for outsiders, or when collapsed entirely into the opposite error of indiscriminate scattering that ignores the Lord's call for discernment.
corruption_paragraphs: Gospel-withholding misreading. Some have abused the proverb to justify refusing to evangelize the hardened, the poor, or the morally repugnant — treating whole classes of sinners as "swine" unworthy of the gospel. This inverts the text. The gospel is freely preached to all (Mark 16:15); the proverb governs the allocation of depth and sacred correction toward those who will not trample them, after they have shown trampling contempt. The dogs and swine are defined by their response (trampling and rending), not by their social class or depth of sin. Christ ate with publicans and sinners; He did not cast His pearls before the scornful Pharisees who had set themselves to destroy Him.

Indiscriminate-scattering misreading. The opposite error treats the proverb as obsolete sentiment and scatters sacred things without discernment: deep discipleship offered to the openly contemptuous, holy correction pressed on the settled scorner, the church's costly investment poured into those who despise it. Proverbs 9:7-8 makes the same point in wisdom terms: reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee. The Lord's own pattern (shaking dust, turning to receptive soil) models the discernment the proverb commands. Wisdom allocates; folly scatters.
roots_summary: From Matthew 7:6; the Lord Jesus's proverb on the discerning allocation of holy things; the dogs and swine are defined by trampling contempt, not social class; paired with Luke 10 dust-shaking and Acts 13 turning to receptive soil.

etymology: From 2 Timothy 2:2, where Paul charges Timothy to commit the deposit of sound teaching "to faithful men" (pistois anthrōpois) who will be able to teach others also. Pistos means trustworthy, reliable, believing — the man who can be entrusted with a deposit and will guard and transmit it.
biblical_def: "Faithful men" is the apostolic term for the trustworthy disciples to whom the deposit of sound doctrine is to be entrusted for transmission across generations. The charge is given to Timothy at 2 Timothy 2:2: "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also." This single verse names four generations of transmission in one line: Paul, Timothy, the faithful men, and the others they will teach. The qualification is twofold — faithfulness (pistos: trustworthy, reliable, proven) and aptness to teach (able to transmit the deposit accurately to others). The verse is the charter of biblical multiplication: the gospel and its sound doctrine are not merely preached to crowds but entrusted, deposit-like, to reliable men who will themselves become entrusters. This is the engine of the Great Commission's depth dimension — not addition (one teacher reaching many hearers) but multiplication (each faithful man producing faithful men who produce faithful men). From the Reformed standpoint, the faithful man is one whom the Spirit has made trustworthy through regeneration and sanctification (1 Cor 4:2, "it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful"), and the deposit he guards is the once-for-all-delivered faith (Jude 3), not a private innovation. The local church's ministerial training, eldership, and discipleship all flow from this verse.
webster_summary: The trustworthy, teaching-apt disciples to whom the deposit of sound doctrine is entrusted for transmission (2 Tim 2:2); the engine of biblical multiplication across four named generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and the others they teach.
webster_full: FAITHFUL MEN, noun phrase. From 2 Timothy 2:2 (pistois anthrōpois).
The trustworthy disciples to whom the deposit of sound teaching is committed for transmission.

The charter of biblical multiplication: four generations in one verse — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and the others they will teach.

1 Corinthians 4:2

Jude 1:3

corruption_summary: Faithful men is corrupted when the qualification of faithfulness is replaced by talent, charisma, or numerical productivity, when the deposit entrusted is treated as a private innovation rather than the once-delivered faith, or when the verse's complementarian specificity (the office of teaching elder) is flattened.
corruption_paragraphs: Talent-over-faithfulness misreading. Modern ministry often selects for charisma, platform, communication skill, or measurable productivity rather than for the proven faithfulness 2 Tim 2:2 requires. The verse names faithfulness first and teaching-aptness second; a brilliant communicator who is not faithful is disqualified, and a faithful man of modest gifts is qualified. 1 Cor 4:2 makes faithfulness the one thing required of a steward. The church that entrusts its deposit to the gifted-but-unfaithful loses the deposit within a generation; the church that entrusts it to the faithful preserves it across centuries.

Innovation-over-deposit misreading. The faithful man transmits a deposit — the things heard from Paul, the faith once delivered to the saints (Jude 3), the good thing committed to Timothy's keeping (2 Tim 1:14). He is not authorized to innovate, update, or improve the deposit; he is to guard and transmit it intact. Progressive and emergent reframings of ministry treat each generation's teachers as authorized to refashion the message for the times. The biblical pattern is conservative in the precise sense: the faithful man conserves the deposit and hands it on unaltered, because it is not his to alter.
roots_summary: From 2 Timothy 2:2; the trustworthy, teaching-apt disciples to whom the deposit of sound doctrine is committed; faithfulness (1 Cor 4:2) is the first qualification; the deposit is the once-delivered faith (Jude 3), not private innovation.

etymology: A discipleship term, drawn from the agricultural and generational imagery of Scripture, distinguishing multiplication (disciples who make disciples who make disciples) from mere addition (one teacher accumulating hearers). Rooted in 2 Timothy 2:2's four-generation chain and the seed-bearing-seed pattern of Genesis 1 and the Gospels.
biblical_def: Spiritual multiplication is the biblical pattern by which the gospel and sound doctrine spread not by addition (one teacher accumulating more hearers) but by multiplication (each disciple becoming a disciple-maker, who produces disciple-makers, across generations). Its charter text is 2 Timothy 2:2, which names four generations of transmission in a single verse: Paul entrusts the deposit to Timothy, who entrusts it to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also. The pattern is woven into creation itself — the seed bearing seed after its kind (Gen 1:11-12) — and into the Lord's own method: He preached to thousands but poured three years of depth into twelve men, who then turned the world upside down (Acts 17:6). The arithmetic is decisive: a teacher who adds reaches a fixed ceiling bounded by his own lifespan and capacity; a teacher who multiplies sets in motion a chain that compounds beyond him. The Great Commission is fulfilled by depth, not merely breadth: "make disciples... teaching them to observe all things" (Matt 28:19-20), so that the taught become teachers. From the Reformed standpoint, the increase belongs to God (1 Cor 3:6-7, "God gave the increase"), and the multiplication is the ordinary fruit of the Spirit working through the ordained means of the Word, the sacraments, and faithful men. Multiplication is not a technique that guarantees results; it is the God-ordained shape of how the kingdom grows through entrusted, transmitted, generation-crossing discipleship.
webster_summary: The biblical pattern by which the gospel spreads through disciples who make disciple-makers across generations (multiplication), not merely a teacher accumulating hearers (addition); charter text 2 Tim 2:2; the increase belongs to God (1 Cor 3:6-7).

The Lord's method: preached to thousands, poured depth into twelve, who turned the world upside down (Acts 17:6).
Reformed anchor: the increase belongs to God (1 Cor 3:6-7); multiplication is the God-ordained shape of kingdom growth, not a guaranteed technique.

corruption_summary: Spiritual multiplication is corrupted when reduced to a guaranteed church-growth technique, when the increase is credited to method or man rather than to God, or when multiplication of numbers is pursued at the expense of the depth and doctrinal fidelity that make a disciple worth multiplying.
corruption_paragraphs: Technique-and-results misreading. The language of multiplication can be absorbed into the church-growth movement as a guaranteed-results methodology: apply the system, get the compounding numbers. The Reformed correction is 1 Cor 3:6-7: Paul plants, Apollos waters, but God gives the increase; neither the planter nor the waterer is anything. Multiplication is the God-ordained shape of how the kingdom grows, not a lever the church pulls to force growth. The faithful man plants and waters and entrusts; the increase is the Lord's gift, given in His measure and timing.

Numbers-over-depth misreading. A multiplication that prizes the rate of numerical reproduction can hollow out the very thing being reproduced, producing many shallow disciples who transmit a thin and drifting message. The biblical pattern multiplies faithful men who guard a deposit (2 Tim 2:2; 2 Tim 1:14): the depth and doctrinal fidelity are the point, and the multiplication carries them forward. A chain that multiplies error multiplies destruction. Better twelve faithful men who guard the deposit than twelve thousand who trample it.
roots_summary: The biblical pattern of disciples making disciple-makers across generations (multiplication, not addition); charter text 2 Tim 2:2; creation pattern of seed bearing seed; the increase belongs to God (1 Cor 3:6-7).

etymology: The single Greek imperative mathēteusate ("make disciples," "disciple") at the heart of the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19). It is the only finite verb of command in the commission; "go," "baptizing," and "teaching" are participles that modify it. From mathētēs, a learner or apprentice.
biblical_def: "Make disciples" is the central command of the Great Commission and, grammatically, the only imperative in it: "Go ye therefore, and teach [make disciples of] all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you" (Matt 28:19-20). In the Greek, the one finite imperative is mathēteusate (make disciples); the surrounding words — going, baptizing, teaching — are participles that describe how the disciple-making is carried out. This grammar matters: the church's commission is not first to go, nor first to baptize, nor first to teach, but to MAKE DISCIPLES, with going, baptizing, and teaching as the means. A disciple (mathētēs) is a learner-apprentice who follows a master, takes his yoke, and is conformed to his life and teaching (Matt 11:29; Luke 6:40, "every one that is perfect shall be as his master"). Disciple-making therefore is not mere decision-eliciting or crowd-gathering; it is the patient formation of apprentices who are baptized into the Triune name and taught to observe all that Christ commanded. The two participles mark the two halves: baptism (the initiatory mark of covenant membership) and teaching-to-observe (the lifelong formation in obedience). From the Reformed standpoint, disciple-making is the ordinary work of the local church through the ordained means of grace, and its scope is all nations — the command is universal in reach and comprehensive in depth ("all things whatsoever I have commanded").
webster_summary: The central command of the Great Commission and its only imperative (Greek mathēteusate, Matt 28:19); going, baptizing, and teaching are the participial means; disciple-making is the patient formation of baptized apprentices taught to observe all Christ commanded.
webster_full: MAKE DISCIPLES, verb phrase. Greek mathēteusate (Matthew 28:19), the only imperative in the Great Commission.
Going, baptizing, and teaching are participles describing how the disciple-making is carried out.

Two participial halves: baptism (initiatory covenant mark) and teaching-to-observe (lifelong formation in obedience). Scope: all nations.

corruption_summary: Make disciples is corrupted when reduced to decision-eliciting or crowd-gathering that stops at conversion, when the going is elevated above the disciple-making it merely modifies, or when the "teaching to observe all things" is trimmed to a comfortable subset of Christ's commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Decision-over-discipleship misreading. Much modern evangelism treats the commission as fulfilled when a decision is secured — a hand raised, a prayer prayed, a card signed. But the imperative is make DISCIPLES, not make decisions; and a disciple is an apprentice formed over time, baptized into the covenant and taught to observe all Christ commanded. Decisional evangelism that gathers crowds and elicits professions without forming obedient apprentices has done the participle (a kind of going and proclaiming) while neglecting the imperative (making disciples). The Lord did not commission us to produce converts but to produce disciples.

Trimmed-teaching misreading. The commission specifies "teaching them to observe ALL THINGS whatsoever I have commanded you" (Matt 28:20). Disciple-making that teaches a comfortable subset — the encouraging commands, the culturally palatable commands — while quietly omitting the hard commands (self-denial, cross-bearing, sexual purity, costly obedience, the narrow way) is not the disciple-making Christ commanded. The faithful church teaches the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), forming apprentices in all that Christ commanded, not in the portions that give no offense.
roots_summary: Greek mathēteusate (Matt 28:19), the only imperative in the Great Commission; going, baptizing, teaching are the participial means; disciple-making is the formation of baptized apprentices taught to observe all Christ commanded.

From mathētēs — a learner-apprentice who follows and is conformed to his master (Luke 6:40)
Modifying participles: poreuthentes (going), baptizontes (baptizing), didaskontes (teaching)
Two halves: baptism (initiatory covenant mark) + teaching to observe all things (lifelong formation)
usage: Make disciples — the central command and only imperative of the Great Commission (Matt 28:19).
Going, baptizing, and teaching are the means; making disciples is the command.
Not decisions but disciples; not a comfortable subset but all things whatsoever Christ commanded.

etymology: Translates the Greek parathēkē ("deposit, that which is entrusted") with the verb phylassō ("guard, keep") from 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 1:14. A paratheke was a treasure entrusted to another for safekeeping, which the trustee was bound to return intact.
biblical_def: "Guard the deposit" is the apostolic charge to Timothy (and through him to every minister and faithful man) to keep intact the entrusted treasure of sound doctrine. The command appears twice in the Pastoral Epistles: "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust" (1 Tim 6:20), and "That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us" (2 Tim 1:14). The Greek paratheke is a banking-and-legal term: a deposit placed in trust, which the trustee is morally and legally bound to guard and return undiminished and unaltered. Applied to doctrine, it means the gospel and the apostolic teaching are not the minister's to revise, update, trim, or improve; they are a trust he must guard intact and hand on whole. The deposit is the faith once delivered to the saints (Jude 3) — complete, closed, and sufficient. The guarding is not done in human strength but "by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us" (2 Tim 1:14): the Spirit who inspired the deposit enables its faithful keeping. This charge is the doctrinal backbone of confessionalism: the church writes confessions and catechisms precisely to guard the deposit against the slow drift, the cultural accommodation, and the fashionable revision that every generation presses upon it. From the Reformed standpoint, guarding the deposit is the first duty of the teaching elder, and the means of grace, the confession, and the faithful man (2 Tim 2:2) are all instruments of that guarding.
webster_summary: The apostolic charge to keep intact the entrusted treasure of sound doctrine (Greek paratheke, 1 Tim 6:20; 2 Tim 1:14); the gospel is a trust to be guarded and handed on whole, not revised; the doctrinal backbone of confessionalism.
webster_full: GUARD THE DEPOSIT, verb phrase. Greek paratheke (deposit) + phylassō (guard), from 1 Timothy 6:20 and 2 Timothy 1:14.
A paratheke was a treasure entrusted for safekeeping, to be returned intact and unaltered.
Applied to doctrine: the gospel and apostolic teaching are a trust to guard whole, not to revise, trim, or improve.
The guarding is done "by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us" (2 Tim 1:14); the deposit is the faith once delivered (Jude 3).
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:20
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.
2 Timothy 1:14
That good thing which was committed unto thee keep by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us.
2 Timothy 1:13
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Jude 1:3
It was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Guard the deposit is corrupted when the deposit is treated as a living tradition open to each generation's revision, when guarding is mistaken for mere preservation without the Spirit's power, or when the charge is used to defend a man's private traditions rather than the apostolic faith once delivered.
corruption_paragraphs: Living-tradition misreading. Progressive and liberal theology recasts the deposit as a developing, living tradition that each generation is authorized to revise for its own context — so that guarding becomes updating. The paratheke metaphor forbids this: a deposit is guarded by being returned intact, not by being improved. The minister who alters the deposit has embezzled the trust. The deposit is the faith ONCE delivered (Jude 3) — the "once" (hapax) means once-for-all, complete, closed. Guarding means handing on the same faith Paul handed to Timothy, unrevised.

Private-tradition misreading. The opposite abuse invokes "guard the deposit" to defend a man's or a movement's private traditions, idiosyncratic readings, or cultural accretions as though they were the apostolic faith. The deposit is specifically the form of sound words heard from the apostle (2 Tim 1:13), the faith once delivered to the saints (Jude 3) — not every conviction a teacher holds dear. Confessions guard the deposit precisely by distinguishing the apostolic faith from private opinion and binding the conscience only to what Scripture teaches.
roots_summary: Greek paratheke (deposit) + phylassō (guard), 1 Tim 6:20; 2 Tim 1:14; the apostolic charge to keep intact the entrusted treasure of sound doctrine, guarded by the Spirit, handed on whole; the backbone of confessionalism.

Verb phylassō — "guard, keep, watch over" (1 Tim 6:20; 2 Tim 1:14)
The deposit = the form of sound words (2 Tim 1:13) and the faith once delivered (Jude 3)
Guarded "by the Holy Ghost which dwelleth in us" (2 Tim 1:14); the doctrinal basis of confessionalism
usage: Guard the deposit — keep intact the entrusted treasure of sound doctrine (1 Tim 6:20; 2 Tim 1:14).
A deposit is guarded by being returned intact, not by being improved.
The faith once delivered — guarding means handing on the same faith unrevised, by the Spirit's power.

etymology: Drawn from the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13; Mark 4; Luke 8), where the seed of the word falls on four soils — wayside, stony, thorny, and good ground. The "good ground" (gē kalē) is the receptive soil that hears, understands, and bears fruit.
biblical_def: "Receptive soil" names the good ground of the Parable of the Sower — the heart that hears the word, understands and receives it, and bears fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (Matt 13:8, 23). In the parable, one seed (the word of the kingdom) meets four soils and yields four results: the wayside where the word is snatched away, the stony ground where it springs up but withers without root, the thorny ground where the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke it, and the good ground that bears fruit (Matt 13:18-23). The receptive soil is distinguished not by the quality of the seed (which is the same in every case) nor by the diligence of the sower (who sows on all soils alike) but by the prepared condition of the heart. The Lord's own interpretation makes the soils representations of how different hearers receive the same preached word. From the Reformed standpoint, the receptivity of the good ground is itself the work of God — the heart the Lord opens (Acts 16:14), the stony heart replaced with a heart of flesh (Ezek 36:26), the ground prepared by the Spirit before the seed lands. The doctrine grounds the discipleship principle of allocating depth toward the receptive: the sower sows broadly (the seed falls on every soil), but the harvest, the fruit, and therefore the worthwhile investment of cultivation come from the good ground. This is the agricultural form of the same truth the son of peace teaches in Luke 10.
webster_summary: The good ground of the Parable of the Sower (Matt 13:8, 23) — the heart that hears, understands, receives, and bears fruit; distinguished not by better seed or sower but by the Spirit-prepared condition of the heart (Acts 16:14; Ezek 36:26).
webster_full: RECEPTIVE SOIL, noun phrase. The "good ground" (gē kalē) of the Parable of the Sower (Matt 13; Mark 4; Luke 8).
The heart that hears the word, understands and receives it, and bears fruit thirty-, sixty-, and a hundredfold (Matt 13:8, 23).
Distinguished not by the seed (same in every case) nor the sower (sows on all soils) but by the prepared condition of the heart.
Reformed anchor: the receptivity is God's work — the heart the Lord opens (Acts 16:14), the heart of flesh given for the heart of stone (Ezek 36:26).
scriptures: Matthew 13:8
But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.
Matthew 13:23
But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Acts 16:14
And a certain woman named Lydia... heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Ezekiel 36:26
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Receptive soil is corrupted when the good ground's fruitfulness is credited to the hearer's native virtue rather than to the Spirit's preparation, when the parable is read as a technique for finding pre-qualified prospects, or when the universal sowing is curtailed because only some soil bears fruit.
corruption_paragraphs: Native-virtue misreading. The good ground is sometimes read as the naturally good-hearted, sincere, or open person — as though the soil prepared itself. The Reformed reading anchors the receptivity in God: Lydia's heart was opened by the Lord (Acts 16:14); the heart of stone is replaced with a heart of flesh by sovereign grace (Ezek 36:26). The good ground is good because God made it good. The parable magnifies the Spirit's preparatory work, not the hearer's native goodness.

Curtailed-sowing misreading. Because only the good ground bears fruit, some conclude the sower should sow only where fruit is likely — preaching only to the pre-qualified. But the parable's sower scatters seed on all four soils; the broad sowing is assumed, not questioned. The lesson is not "sow selectively" but "expect varied results, and do not be discouraged when much seed does not bear." The discipleship principle of allocating depth toward the receptive (the son of peace, the good ground) never curtails the universal sowing of the word; it governs where the sustained cultivation goes after the seed has been broadly cast.
roots_summary: The good ground of the Parable of the Sower (Matt 13:8, 23); the heart that hears, understands, receives, and bears fruit; receptivity is God's preparatory work (Acts 16:14; Ezek 36:26); the agricultural form of the son-of-peace principle.
roots_lines: Greek gē kalē (Matt 13:8) — "good ground," the fourth and fruitful soil
The four soils: wayside (snatched), stony (no root), thorny (choked), good (fruitful) — Matt 13:18-23
Distinguished by the prepared heart, not by better seed or more diligent sowing
Reformed anchor: the heart the Lord opens (Acts 16:14); the heart of flesh for the heart of stone (Ezek 36:26)
usage: Receptive soil — the good ground that hears, understands, receives, and bears fruit (Matt 13:23).
The same seed, the same sower; the difference is the Spirit-prepared condition of the heart.
Broad sowing on all soils; sustained cultivation toward the good ground — the agricultural form of the son-of-peace principle.

etymology: The apostolic missionary partnership of Paul (formerly Saul of Tarsus) and Barnabas ("son of consolation," Acts 4:36, originally Joseph the Levite of Cyprus), commissioned together by the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1-3) for the first missionary journey.
biblical_def: Paul and Barnabas were the apostolic missionary partnership commissioned by the church at Antioch for the first missionary journey (Acts 13-14), and a model of both the strategy of turning toward receptive soil and the sober reality that even faithful partnerships can divide. Barnabas ("son of consolation") first appears selling his field for the church (Acts 4:36-37), then vouching for the newly-converted Saul when the Jerusalem church feared him (Acts 9:27), then being sent to shepherd the new Antioch church and fetching Saul to help (Acts 11:22-26). The church at Antioch, by the Spirit's direction, set the two apart: "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them" (Acts 13:2). On the journey, at Pisidian Antioch, after the Jews contradicted and blasphemed, the two enacted the allocation principle: "It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you... lo, we turn to the Gentiles" (Acts 13:46). They did not stop preaching; they redirected their labor from persistent rejecters toward receptive soil, and "the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region" (Acts 13:49). Yet the partnership later divided sharply over John Mark, who had deserted them earlier: "the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other" (Acts 15:39). Barnabas took Mark; Paul took Silas. Providentially, the division doubled the mission, and Mark was later restored to Paul's esteem (2 Tim 4:11, "profitable to me for the ministry"). The partnership teaches strategy, grace toward the receptive, and the honest truth that godly men may part ways without either being a villain.
webster_summary: The apostolic missionary partnership commissioned at Antioch (Acts 13:1-3); model of turning toward receptive soil after rejection (Acts 13:46) and of the sober reality that faithful men may divide (over John Mark, Acts 15:39), a division God used to double the mission.
webster_full: PAUL AND BARNABAS, proper noun. The apostolic missionary partnership of the first journey (Acts 13-14).
Barnabas ("son of consolation," Acts 4:36): sold his field, vouched for Saul (Acts 9:27), shepherded Antioch and fetched Saul (Acts 11:22-26).
Commissioned by the Spirit through the Antioch church (Acts 13:2); enacted the turn to receptive soil at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:46).
Later divided sharply over John Mark (Acts 15:39); the division doubled the mission; Mark was restored to Paul's esteem (2 Tim 4:11).
scriptures: Acts 13:2-3

As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them. And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Acts 13:46

Then Paul and Barnabas waxed bold, and said, It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.
Acts 15:39
And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus.
2 Timothy 4:11
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry.
corruption_summary: Paul and Barnabas are corrupted when their turn to the Gentiles is read as abandoning the Jews, when their sharp division is sentimentalized away or used to excuse factiousness, or when Barnabas is reduced to a footnote to Paul rather than honored as the man who first vouched for him.
corruption_paragraphs: Abandonment misreading. "Lo, we turn to the Gentiles" (Acts 13:46) is sometimes read as a wholesale abandonment of the Jewish people. The text is more careful: the word was spoken to the Jews FIRST (the apostolic pattern, Rom 1:16, "to the Jew first"), and only after persistent contradiction and blasphemy did they redirect their labor. Paul continued to grieve and pray for his kinsmen (Rom 9:1-3; 10:1) and to enter synagogues first in city after city. The turn is the allocation principle (redirect depth toward receptive soil), not the abandonment of any people.

Division-sentimentalized misreading. Some treatments either airbrush the sharp contention over John Mark or, worse, cite it to excuse church factiousness as normal and inevitable. The text is honest without being cynical: two godly men disagreed sharply over a real question (whether to take the man who had deserted them), they parted, and God overruled the parting for good — the mission doubled, and Mark was later restored. The episode neither pretends mature believers never clash nor treats the clash as a model to imitate. It shows the providence of God working even through the friction of faithful men.
roots_summary: The apostolic missionary partnership of the first journey (Acts 13-14); commissioned at Antioch; enacted the turn to receptive soil (Acts 13:46); divided over John Mark (Acts 15:39), a division God used to double the mission.

usage: Paul and Barnabas — the missionary partnership commissioned at Antioch for the first journey (Acts 13).

etymology: A U.S.M.C. Ministries framing for the biblical office of the father as the appointed head and watchman of his household. "Captain" draws on the military image of the officer responsible for the readiness, discipline, and welfare of those under his command; here applied to the father standing watch over his home. Coined by editor Adam Johns; rooted in the headship and household-government passages of Scripture.
biblical_def: The "family captain" is the U.S.M.C. Ministries framing for the biblical truth that the father is the appointed head, shepherd, and watchman of his household — the man who stands watch over his home and bears first responsibility for its spiritual readiness. The framing gathers several biblical strands. The father is the covenant head who must "command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD" (Gen 18:19, of Abraham). He is the one charged to teach the words of God diligently to his children, talking of them when he sits in his house and walks by the way (Deut 6:6-7). He is the household-governor whose qualification for church office is precisely that he "ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity" (1 Tim 3:4). He is the Joshua who declares for his whole house, "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Josh 24:15). The captain image carries the weight of the office: a captain is responsible for the readiness, discipline, provision, and welfare of those under his command, and he answers for them. The first discipleship cohort is therefore not the church program but the household; the first place a man disciples is his own table. From the Reformed and complementarian standpoint, this is not domineering but sacrificial headship modeled on Christ's love for the church (Eph 5:25), a stewardship the father holds on loan and will give account for. A man who will not disciple at his own table will not disciple anywhere; the family captain begins there.
webster_summary: U.S.M.C. Ministries framing for the biblical office of the father as appointed head and watchman of his household (Gen 18:19; Deut 6:6-7; Josh 24:15; 1 Tim 3:4); sacrificial headship modeled on Christ (Eph 5:25); the household is a man's first discipleship cohort.
webster_full: FAMILY CAPTAIN, noun phrase. U.S.M.C. Ministries framing for the father as appointed head and watchman of his household.

Biblical strands: the covenant head who commands his household in the way of the LORD (Gen 18:19); the father who teaches God's words diligently (Deut 6:6-7); the household-governor qualified for office by ruling his own house well (1 Tim 3:4); the Joshua who declares for his whole house (Josh 24:15).
The captain image: responsible for readiness, discipline, provision, and welfare; he answers for those under his command.
Sacrificial headship modeled on Christ's love for the church (Eph 5:25), held on loan, to be given account for. The household is a man's first discipleship cohort.
Coined by editor Adam Johns; the Family Captain framework anchors U.S.M.C. Ministries' men's discipleship.
scriptures: Genesis 18:19

For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment; that the LORD may bring upon Abraham that which he hath spoken of him.
Deuteronomy 6:6-7

And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Joshua 24:15
And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Ephesians 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.
corruption_summary: The family captain is corrupted when headship is twisted into domineering control rather than sacrificial service, when the egalitarian spirit of the age dissolves the father's distinct office of household leadership, or when the father abdicates the office entirely and leaves the spiritual formation of his home to his wife, the church program, or no one.
corruption_paragraphs: Domineering misreading. Fallen men readily twist headship into harshness, control, and the gratification of self — the very thing Scripture forbids. Biblical headship is cruciform: the husband loves his wife as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it (Eph 5:25), and the father provokes not his children to wrath but brings them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4). The captain who lords it over his household has abandoned the model. The office is authority exercised as sacrificial service, answerable to Christ the Head, not a license for domination.

Egalitarian-dissolution and abdication misreadings. The spirit of the age presses two opposite errors. The first dissolves the father's distinct office altogether, treating household leadership as an interchangeable, genderless function — the egalitarian rejection of the creational order (the dictionary's biblical-order and biblical-egalitarianism entries draw the line). The second, more common in practice, is simple abdication: the father present in body but absent in spiritual leadership, leaving the discipleship of his home to his wife, the youth program, or no one. Scripture holds the father responsible (Gen 18:19; Deut 6:7; Eph 6:4). The family-captain framing exists to recall men to an office the culture has both denied in theory and abandoned in practice.
roots_summary: U.S.M.C. Ministries framing for the father as appointed head and watchman of his household; biblical strands from Gen 18:19, Deut 6:6-7, Josh 24:15, 1 Tim 3:4; cruciform headship modeled on Christ (Eph 5:25); the household is a man's first discipleship cohort.
